data.title: Canada Deems Vancouver Port Expansion a National Priority in Bid to Diversify Trade — Update
data.description:
By Paul Vieira 




  OTTAWA--Canada declared as a national priority a proposed expansion at the country's busiest port in Vancouver, British Columbia, arguing that it is required for the country to meet its goal of doubling non-U.S. exports by 2035. 



  The designation also kicks off an accelerated regulatory review process, whereby officials are tasked with determining how the expansion proceeds and under what conditions, as opposed to whether it requires approval. 



  Officials said this puts the timing for a final investment decision from the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority by mid-2027. 



  "We cannot afford to let bottlenecks hold back Canadian trade," Canadian Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said Friday at a press conference in suburban Vancouver. "The sooner we build the [trade] capacity Canada needs, the sooner Canadian businesses and workers can benefit." 



  The authority, which manages the Vancouver port, said the expansion project would increase container capacity by about 50%, through a new land-mass and wharf structure covering 300 acres. This additional capacity could support annual trade of 100 billion Canadian dollars (US$71.5 billion). 



  Officials peg the project's cost at C$5.9 billion. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has pledged up to C$10 billion in financial support for Pacific coast trade corridors. 



  The port authority said the Vancouver terminal currently handles more than C$1 billion in commerce daily, and more cargo than the next five largest Canadian ports combined. 



  The expansion, upgrade and construction of trade corridors across Canada is a priority initiative for Carney, who has argued that it is necessary to restore resilience in the economy and reduce the country's reliance on U.S. trade to drive economic growth. 



  According to government documents, there needs to be a "significant expansion" of Canada's port capacity to diversify trade, adding that 80% of trade with non-U.S. markets is done by sea. The prime minister has set a goal of doubling the level of non-U.S. exports by 2035. 



  "Continued inaction on port expansion could eventually force Canadian importers and exporters to utilize U.S. ports--a dependency that is untenable in the current geopolitical circumstances," officials said, according to documents distributed at a technical briefing. "Port expansion is thus integral to ensuring Canadian sovereignty and control over key economic linkages to the rest of the world," the officials said, according to the documents. 



  Officials warned that without port expansion, Canada could face sharply higher shipping costs of up to C$900 million a year due to traffic congestion and insufficient capacity. 



  Bank of Canada researchers warned this year that the country lacked the port capacity to executive the government's trade agenda. 



  The central bank's analysis indicated Canadian ports can't accommodate some of the latest ultra-large container ships being deployed. Because of this, some goods originating from China and destined for Canada and loaded onto these big vessels have to dock in Los Angeles--and those goods could be subject to U.S. tariffs. 





  Write to Paul Vieira at paul.vieira@wsj.com 





  (END) Dow Jones Newswires

data.title: Killingly Public Schools - Notice of Data Incident
data.description:
Killingly Public Schools - Notice of Data Incident

Killingly Public Schools - Notice of Data Incident

PR Newswire

HARTFORD, Conn., Oct. 30, 2026

HARTFORD, Conn., Oct. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Killingly Public Schools ("KPS"), a school district located in Killingly, Connecticut, was the victim of a recent data privacy incident involving certain personally identifiable information ("PII").

What Happened: In October 2025, KPS detected a disruption to its computer network. Upon learning of the activity, KPS took immediate action to secure its systems which included taking parts of its network offline. KPS partnered with cybersecurity specialists to restore its network and investigate the nature and scope of the event. The investigation determined that certain data was accessed on its network without authorization. KPS then conducted a thorough review of the data to identify what personal information, if any, was contained in the potentially affected files and to whom that information belonged. KPS thereafter commenced a comprehensive review to determine whose information was contained within those files, which concluded on September 23, 2026.

What KPS is Doing: Upon learning of the event, KPS took immediate action to contain and remediate the issue, including taking parts of its network offline. However, core services were restored the same day. KPS partnered with cybersecurity specialists to thoroughly investigate the incident and notified federal law enforcement. KPS reset account passwords and continues to utilize multi-factor authentication for its systems. Additionally, KPS is assessing its existing security safeguards and policies for ways it can strengthen its systems and increase resilience against evolving threats.    

What You Can Do: To date, KPS has no evidence of misuse of any PII for fraud or identity theft. However, as a general matter, it is best practice to remain vigilant for incidents of identity theft and fraud, from any source, by reviewing and monitoring your account statements and free credit reports for suspicious activity and errors. If you discover any suspicious or unusual activity on your accounts, promptly contact your financial institution or the service provider.

Additional information about the incident and resources one may consider taking advantage of, should they feel it appropriate to do so, may be found on the Killingly Public Schools website at: https://www.killinglyschools.org/.

Nicholas Jajko (Nicholas.Jajko@kennedyslaw.com) and Annie Jaffee (Annie.Jaffee@kennedyslaw.com)

data.title: Metropolitan issues statement on State Water Board adoption of Bay-Delta Water Quality Control Plan
data.description:
Metropolitan issues statement on State Water Board adoption of Bay-Delta Water Quality Control Plan

Metropolitan Water District General Manager Shivaji Deshmukh issues the following statement on the State Water Resources Control Board’s adoption of an update to the Bay-Delta Water Quality Control Plan:

“Metropolitan and partners across the state have worked for years to develop a smarter approach to building a healthier Bay-Delta and a more reliable water future for California, recognizing that flows alone are insufficient to protect the estuary’s ecosystem and the state’s water supply. The result – the Healthy Rivers and Landscapes Program – was intended to bring together additional water, habitat restoration and science, though a new governance structure and dedicated funding, to dramatically change how the Bay-Delta is managed. Implementation of the Healthy Rivers and Landscapes Program would be a landmark achievement in moving toward collaborative, science-based decision making to improve the health of the Bay-Delta while providing reliable water for California communities and businesses.

“Metropolitan appreciates the State Water Board’s commitment to a sustainable Bay-Delta and its efforts to include in the plan an implementation pathway that does not rely primarily on flows. However, Metropolitan is disappointed in the plan adopted yesterday. Ultimately, the State Water Board did not adequately incorporate the pathway as envisioned by the Healthy Rivers and Landscapes Program.

“Metropolitan will continue its review, including the changes incorporated into the adopted plan, to determine crucial next steps, and while doing that will continue to collaborate and engage agencies and partners. Metropolitan remains committed to the principles of the HRL Program and to finding solutions together. Southern California’s water future is closely connected to the health of the Bay-Delta, and our shared goals remain as important as ever.”
